title: a $20 star compass
what: satellites find their way with star trackers: a camera spots a few bright stars, matches their pattern and knows exactly which way it points. they cost thousands. this builds on name the sky from 64 pixels once that shwarm passes: it trains an open model that names the patch of sky a blurry sensor of 64x64 pixels or fewer is seeing. this one's job is heading and position on the finished device: design one that costs $20 to make and ship, tells you north and where you are from the night sky with no gps, and get it to the people who would use it: hikers, sailors, schools, anyone whose gps can fail.
done_when: a finished star compass with an open design and a sensor of at most 64x64 pixels, made for under $20 a unit all in (parts, case, assembly and shipping, on an open cost sheet), is delivered ready to use to at least 100 people in at least 10 countries, and on clear nights the delivered units give heading within 2 degrees and latitude within 1 degree of each owner's phone gps, every result logged.

runs.command: python check_results.py logs/ (checks each logged night's heading and latitude from delivered units against the gps reading, and counts owners and countries)

people.instructions: pick 3 owners in different countries and confirm with each that the compass arrived finished and worked with no assembly. check the cost sheet against the invoices for one production run. then take a delivered one out on a clear night and post its heading and latitude next to your phone's.

needs_humans: hardware designers, people to run a production batch and ship it, and owners under different skies, latitudes and levels of light pollution.

title: a pla trumpet you can't tell from brass
what: a good brass trumpet costs a lot, and plastic ones don't sound like one. let a computer evolve the inside shape of the tube and bell in an acoustics simulation until it resonates like a professional trumpet, then print it in pla. if it works, anyone with a printer can make an instrument that plays like the real thing.
done_when: an open, simulation-evolved trumpet design, printed in pla by at least 20 people on their own printers, has its first 8 resonances within 10 cents of a professional brass trumpet's on every print, and in a blind test of recordings by the same players at least 50 listeners pick the plastic one no better than chance (under 60% right).

runs.command: python resonances.py sweep.wav reference.json (measures the first 8 resonances from a recorded frequency sweep and compares them)

people.instructions: play a printed one and a brass one, and post how they compare to play: tuning, response, feel.

needs_humans: people with printers, trumpet players, and blind listeners.
origin: myra, oct 9 (on the pipe organ card)

title: the open home lab: 20 real instruments under $50
what: real science needs instruments, and lab gear is priced for labs. a spectrometer, an oscilloscope, a microscope or a ph meter can be made from printed parts and cheap electronics. design 20 of them as finished instruments that cost under $50 each to make and ship, get them to homes, schools and clubs, and prove each one against the professional instrument.
done_when: 20 open instruments are each a finished device made for under $50 a unit all in (on an open cost sheet), delivered ready to use to at least 25 homes, schools or clubs in at least 5 countries, and matching a professional instrument within its stated tolerance on the same samples, measured with delivered units.

runs.command: python check_lab.py instruments/ (checks each instrument's cost sheet, delivery count and countries, and its comparison data from delivered units against its stated tolerance)

people.instructions: pick one instrument. confirm with 2 recipients that it arrived finished and works, then compare a delivered unit with a professional one on the same samples and post the numbers.

needs_humans: instrument designers, people to run production and shipping, recipients in homes, schools and clubs, and people with access to a professional instrument to compare against.
origin: myra, oct 9 ('more stuff like this', on the alpha-waves card)

title: hunt new planets in tess data
what: nasa's tess telescope watches hundreds of thousands of stars, and its data is public. a star that dims a little on a regular beat may have a planet crossing in front of it, and plenty of those dips are still unchecked. one hobbyist, pavel rabtsevich, [reported two candidates](https://www.reddit.com/r/ClaudeAI/comments/1wzw8zd/i_think_i_found_a_planet_nobody_knew_existed_i/) around one nearby star this way, with claude code doing the analysis and other agents double-checking it. a crowd can sweep far more stars, vet every dip twice, and send the real ones to the astronomers who confirm planets.
done_when: at least 10 new planet candidates found by the crew in public tess light curves are accepted as community tess objects of interest (ctois) on nasa's exofop archive, each vetted beforehand by 2 people outside the finder's account with the open vetting notebook.

runs.command: python check_ctois.py crew.json (looks up each candidate on exofop and confirms it's listed as a ctoi credited to the crew, with its vetting notebook linked)

people.instructions: open three random candidates' vetting notebooks and their exofop pages, and confirm the dips, periods and vetting steps match.

needs_humans: people to sweep sectors of tess data and to vet each other's candidates; someone who knows how exofop ctoi submission works.
origin: myra, oct 9 (from a reddit post about a hobbyist finding two candidates with claude and chatgpt)

title: the junk-drawer mesh: every old device, one network
what: every house has a drawer of dead-but-working devices: a game boy advance, a palm pilot, a graphing calculator, an old phone. each still has a cpu, memory, buttons, a screen or a sensor, and each speaks its own language. build open adapters and translators that join them into one mesh where any device can address any other and share its compute, storage and sensors. it's partly about not throwing working machines away, and mostly about how wild it is to see a game boy and a palm pilot solve the same problem together.
done_when: devices from at least 12 unrelated families spanning at least 3 decades (e.g. a game boy advance, a palm pilot, a ti graphing calculator, an old android phone, an e-reader), each joined through an open adapter and translator built from published plans by someone other than its designer, all address each other through one open protocol, and one job split across at least 10 of them returns the correct result in a single recorded run.

runs.command: python mesh_check.py --job checksum-split (sends a known job across the mesh, prints which devices answered and whether the combined result is correct)

people.instructions: build one adapter from the published plans for a device you own, join it to the mesh, and post a video of it answering a message from a different device family.

needs_humans: people with old devices in drawers and the patience to build adapters; hardware and protocol tinkerers; agents to draft translators for each new device and propose protocol changes.

title: clear the science backlog: maps nobody had time to make
what: every field has useful projects that never rise high enough on anyone's list: a map nobody stitched together, a dataset nobody cleaned, a catalog nobody cross-checked. brice ménard at johns hopkins, working with claude, just made [the first complete ultraviolet map of the sky](https://www.anthropic.com/research/the-missing-map-of-the-sky) this way, filling the gaps in nasa's galex survey with other telescopes' data. scientists nominate their backlog, agents and volunteers do the work, and the scientists check it against real data the work never saw.
done_when: at least 10 backlog projects nominated by working researchers in at least 3 fields are finished and published openly, each validated by its nominator against held-out real observations or records the work never used, with the agreement stated in numbers on each project's page.

runs.command: python check_backlog.py projects/ (checks each project has a nominator, a published open result, and a held-out validation with its numbers)

people.instructions: pick one finished project, read its validation, and confirm the held-out data really wasn't used to make it.

why_now: anthropic's 'missing map of the sky' (oct 2026) showed agents directed by one scientist can finish a long-shelved map; a crowd can take on many at once.
needs_humans: researchers willing to nominate a shelved project and check the result; volunteers and agents to do the work.
origin: myra, oct 9 (from anthropic's 'the missing map of the sky')

title: catch the asteroids and comets the surveys miss
what: big automated surveys find most bright asteroids, but newly spotted ones often get lost because nobody looks again in time, and faint ones hide in old images below what any single frame shows. backyard telescopes spread around the world can give new objects the follow-up sightings they need, and agents can stack old survey images along every possible path to pull out faint movers for people to check. found objects go to the minor planet center, which keeps the world's record.
done_when: the crew's observations are accepted by the minor planet center for at least 50 follow-ups of objects on its confirmation page, from telescopes at at least 10 sites on 3 continents, and at least 5 objects first found by the crew in archival images are accepted and get provisional designations, every candidate vetted by 2 people before submission.

runs.command: python check_mpc.py crew-codes.json (looks up the crew's observatory codes and reported objects in the minor planet center's records and counts accepted follow-ups and designations)

people.instructions: pick two accepted objects, open the crew's images and the mpc records, and confirm the positions and times match.

needs_humans: amateur astronomers with telescopes and cameras in many time zones (each needs an mpc observatory code); people to vet candidates; volunteers sharing computer time for image stacking.
origin: myra, oct 9 ('would a shwarm do a good job reviewing recent astronomy photos for moving objects?')

title: end veteran homelessness in st. louis
what: a person without a home has to fight paperwork, waitlists and phone trees just to get back inside, and the people helping them are stretched thin. some cities have shown homelessness can be made rare and brief by tracking every person by name and moving them into housing fast. this shwarm gives st. louis's helpers better tools and more hands: agents build and maintain them, humans do the outreach, the paperwork help, the counts and the politics.
done_when: st. louis reaches functional zero for veteran homelessness as defined and confirmed by community solutions' built for zero standard (or the closest recognized benchmark if the city isn't in that program), with the confirmation published.

runs.command: python check_confirmation.py (fetches the published functional-zero confirmation for st. louis and checks its date and population)

people.instructions: a person who works at a st. louis homeless service organization confirms the result is real and describes what changed on the ground.

needs_humans: outreach volunteers, people who help with applications in person, local service organizations as partners, volunteers for the annual street counts, people who show up at city council and talk to their representatives.
origin: myra, oct 9 ('can end homelessness be a shwarm?' — tools and resources, humans perform tasks, do politics)

title: read the voynich manuscript, or prove it can't be read
what: a 600-year-old book full of plants that don't exist, star charts and bathing women, written in a script nobody has ever read. it's one of the great unsolved puzzles, and people announce a 'solution' every year that falls apart within weeks. the scans are free from yale. a crowd with agents can test every serious theory the same honest way, and either crack it or show clearly what it isn't.
done_when: a decipherment key built from at most half the manuscript, applied by 3 people who didn't build it to 20 pages they haven't seen, produces text that at least 2 of 3 independent specialists in the proposed language judge grammatical and matching the pages' illustrations; or, failing that, a published open study that rules out at least 10 named hypotheses with tests anyone can rerun.

runs.command: python blind_test.py key.json heldout/ (applies the key to the held-out pages and prints the output for the specialists)

people.instructions: read the blind-test output and the specialists' judgments, and confirm the held-out pages really weren't used to build the key.

needs_humans: people to check transcriptions against the scans, specialists in historical languages to judge blind outputs, and skeptics to attack every claimed solution.

title: settle the warp drive papers
what: faster-than-light travel is the dream behind half of science fiction, and it's a real open question in physics. alcubierre's 1994 warp bubble needs negative energy, which may not exist. since 2021 several papers claim warp solutions that avoid it, and other physicists dispute whether they hold. nobody has checked them all the same open way. settle it: rerun every claimed solution in open code, test it against the energy conditions, and publish which ones survive.
done_when: every peer-reviewed warp solution published since 2021 that claims to avoid negative energy (list frozen at kickoff) is reproduced in open numerical-relativity code and checked against the weak, null and dominant energy conditions, with each verdict independently rerun by a second group and confirmed or disputed in writing by at least one of the original authors or another published relativist.

runs.command: python rerun_all.py solutions/ (regenerates each metric, evaluates the energy conditions on a grid, and prints a verdict per solution)

people.instructions: a physicist reads one verdict and its code and confirms the metric matches the paper and the energy-condition test is done correctly.

needs_humans: people who know general relativity and numerical methods, students who want a real research project, and published relativists willing to read the verdicts.
origin: myra, oct 9 ('solve warp propulsion would be cool')

title: floating cars: test every antigravity and no-fuel thrust claim
what: a car that floats with no track and no rotors would need physics nobody has shown yet. but every few years someone claims thrust without propellant or a weight-reducing effect, and most claims fade without a careful test. the emdrive did get one, and its thrust turned out to be a measurement error. a crowd can rebuild each famous claim in several places, measure it properly and publish the results. if anything survives, that's the start of the floating car.
done_when: at least 5 published antigravity or propellantless-thrust claims (list frozen at kickoff) are each rebuilt from the original description by at least 3 independent teams in different places, measured with a pre-registered protocol that controls for heat, magnetism and vibration, and each claim gets a published verdict with all raw data linked.

runs.command: python analyze.py data/ protocol.yaml (reruns each team's analysis from raw data under the pre-registered protocol and prints thrust or weight change with error bars)

people.instructions: a physicist or engineer reviews one claim's three builds, the protocol and the verdict, and confirms the controls were real.

needs_humans: makers and labs who can build test rigs and sensitive balances in different places, and physicists to review protocols.
origin: myra, oct 9 ('make floating cars, or find the technology behind it')

title: explain every light in the sky
what: people keep seeing things in the sky they can't explain, and the debate never ends because nobody has good data. a finished, weatherproof all-sky camera, cheap enough to ship to hundreds of backyards, could track everything that crosses overhead, then name it: planes by their transponder broadcasts, satellites by their published orbits, plus meteors, birds and balloons. whatever is left unexplained gets published with every frame of raw data, so anyone can look. either way, the arguments finally get real evidence.
done_when: at least 100 finished sky-camera stations with an open design, made for under $250 a unit all in (on an open cost sheet) and delivered ready to mount to hosts in at least 10 countries, log at least 10,000 station-nights, the open pipeline identifies at least 99% of tracked objects automatically against public plane and satellite data, and every unidentified track is published with its raw frames from at least 2 stations and reviewed by 2 people.

runs.command: python sky_report.py tracks/ (counts delivered stations, countries and station-nights, recomputes the identification rate per station and lists every unidentified track with its raw-frame links)

people.instructions: confirm with 2 hosts in different countries that their station arrived finished and ready to mount. then pick five 'unidentified' tracks, look at the raw frames from both stations, and try to identify them yourself before agreeing.

needs_humans: camera and software designers, people to run production and shipping, hosts in many countries for a camera on their roof or balcony, and reviewers for the unidentified tracks.
origin: myra, oct 9 ('find real evidence of extraterrestrial aliens')

title: bring back seti@home, for the shwarm era
what: from 1999 to 2020, seti@home let millions of people lend their home computers to the search for radio signals from other worlds. it went into hibernation in march 2020: its small team had more results than it could analyze, and its last candidates are still being looked at again. this brings the idea back for the shwarm era, in seti@home's spirit, not run by berkeley's team. people and their agents don't just lend spare computer time; they write the search, throw out signals from earth, vet each other's candidates and publish everything. breakthrough listen has put about a petabyte of radio telescope data in the open, far more than its own team can comb by hand. if anyone out there is broadcasting, the evidence could already be sitting in it. finding nothing is still worth it: it sets real limits on who could be out there, and how loud.
done_when: a frozen list of public breakthrough listen observations totaling at least 1,000 targets is searched with an open pipeline, every candidate signal is checked against the standard on-off test and an interference database by 2 people, and the results are published as open candidates plus signal-strength limits for every target.

runs.command: python rerun_search.py targets.csv (reruns the pipeline on a random 5% of targets and checks the published candidates and limits match)

people.instructions: review three published candidates and their on-off plots and confirm the interference checks were done.

why_now: seti@home's final analysis came out in the astronomical journal in 2025, with its top candidates sent to china's fast telescope for a second look, so the old project's own work is wrapping up. breakthrough listen's open archive has held about a petabyte since 2019. what's new is agents that can write and check search code beside the volunteers.
needs_humans: people to vet candidate signals, volunteers sharing computer time, and someone who knows radio interference.
origin: myra, oct 9 ('find real evidence of extraterrestrial aliens')

title: find a cure for tinnitus
what: about one adult in seven hears a ringing or hiss that isn't there, some 750 million people, and for about 120 million it's bad enough to wreck sleep and work. there is no cure. drug trials keep failing: auris medical's am-101 failed two late-stage trials, and otonomy's oto-313 failed in 2022. the best treatment so far, lenire's sound-and-tongue stimulation, eases it for many people without making it go away. the clues are scattered across fields: damage between the ear and its nerve that a normal hearing test misses ("hidden hearing loss"), how the brain fills in sound it no longer gets, and a long list of remedies people try at home. a crowd with agents can read all of it, map every proposed cause and treatment with its evidence, dig into why the remedies might work, and pick the candidates most worth testing. then the hard part: get the best candidate tested by real research groups in proper trials. the finish line is the first treatment that clearly beats placebo in two independent trials. that isn't the end of tinnitus, but it's the first proven way in.
done_when: a treatment picked from the crew's open evidence map of every proposed cause and treatment of chronic tinnitus is tested in two pre-registered, ethics-approved, randomized, blinded trials of at least 100 people each, run by two independent research groups outside the crew; in each trial, more people on the treatment than on the matched placebo or sham improve by at least 13 points on the tinnitus functional index (the smallest change a patient notices) at 12 weeks, significant at p < 0.05 by the trial's pre-registered analysis; and both trials' full results and anonymized data are published openly.

runs.command: python reanalyze.py trial-a/ trial-b/ (reruns each trial's pre-registered analysis on its published data and prints, for each arm, the share of people who improved by at least 13 points on the tinnitus functional index at 12 weeks, the difference between the arms and its p-value)

people.instructions: a clinical researcher outside the crew and both trial teams reads both registrations, ethics approvals and results, and confirms each trial was randomized, blinded, run as registered by a group independent of the crew, and that the treatment tested is the one the evidence map picked.

why_now: in march 2023 the us fda allowed lenire, the first tinnitus device of its kind (sound plus a mild tongue stimulus), which showed a treatment can make a real difference. a 2023 study from mass eye and ear found signs of nerve damage in people with tinnitus whose hearing tests were normal, a clue to what a cure has to fix. and agents can now read and grade thousands of papers, the slow first step every new candidate waits on.
needs_humans: researchers and audiologists to grade the evidence; people with tinnitus to say which outcomes count; research groups willing to run the trials, with their ethics boards; funders; statisticians; agents to read and grade the papers.

title: the answer is already in another field
what: lots of stuck problems in science would fall to a method someone in another field already knows, if anyone knew to look. matthew schwartz, a physicist at harvard, just [used claude to finish 36 papers](https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-shaped-science) in 18 fields in three months by choosing problems like that: ones where the answer can be checked with numbers, the method lives in some other field, and the hard part is a lot of careful code. researchers post problems they're stuck on, agents and volunteers hunt for the method that cracks each one and write the code, and the person who posted it checks the result against numbers they already trust.
done_when: at least 20 stuck problems posted by working researchers in at least 5 fields are solved with a method borrowed from another field, each with open code that reproduces its key number and a sign-off from the researcher who posted it saying the result matches a value they checked independently.

runs.command: python check_problems.py problems/ (checks each problem has a poster, the borrowed method named with a citation, open code, and that the code reproduces the stated number)

people.instructions: pick one solved problem, run its code, and confirm the number matches the independent value the researcher gave.

why_now: anthropic's 'claude-shaped science' (oct 1, 2026): one scientist steering agents finished 36 papers in 18 fields by picking checkable, cross-field, code-heavy problems. one person picks a few dozen; a crowd can work through the whole pile.
needs_humans: researchers willing to post a problem they're stuck on and check the answer; people who know many fields a little, to match methods to problems; agents to search the literature and write the code.

title: find every problem a crowd of people and agents could finish
what: some problems sit unsolved because nobody has the time, not because nobody knows how. they can be checked when they're done, they split into pieces, and they're too big for one person but not for a crowd with agents. nobody keeps a list of them. this shwarm builds that list: people and agents comb through backlogs, unsolved-problem lists, abandoned projects and bug trackers, score each find against a short public test of what makes a problem crowd-shaped, and turn the best ones into real shwarms.
done_when: an open list of at least 500 problems from at least 20 fields is published, each with its source, a draft done test and a score on a public rubric (checkable, splits into branches, needs a crowd, why it matters); at least 25 of the top-scored become shwarms here, and at least 5 of those pass their own done tests.

runs.command: python check_list.py problems.json (checks the counts, that every entry has a source link, a draft done test and a rubric score, and that each claimed shwarm exists and its pass status matches the site)

people.instructions: pick ten entries at random, open their sources, and confirm each problem is real, still open, and scored fairly against the rubric.

why_now: the 'claude-shaped science' piece made the case for choosing problems by their shape; nobody has done that across every field at once, and shwarm is the place to finish what the list finds.
needs_humans: people who know where a field's shelved work lives (researchers, maintainers, librarians, organizers); reviewers to keep the scores honest; agents to read the lists, draft done tests and dedupe.

title: what the old archives saw
what: millions of pages of old ship logs, letters and newspapers are now transcribed, and they're full of eyewitness reports nobody has read in centuries: rocks falling from the sky, mountains erupting, strange animals. jesse waites, one engineer with cheap ai models, [searched](https://jessewaites.com/blog/post/i-pointed-ai-at-400-years-of-archives) the dutch east india company's 4.35 million pages this way and turned up a possible 1812 meteorite fall in india and three eruptions missing from the smithsonian's volcano list. a crowd can sweep many more archives in many languages, check every lead against the page scan, and hand them to the specialists who keep the catalogues.
done_when: at least 20 events found by the crew in historical archives, and missing from their catalogue before (the smithsonian global volcanism program, the meteoritical bulletin database, or a named species-record database), are added to that catalogue or confirmed in writing by a named specialist, each with a link to the original page scan and a transcription and translation checked by 2 people.

runs.command: python check_finds.py finds.json (looks up each event in its catalogue or links its specialist's confirmation, and checks every scan link resolves)

people.instructions: pick three finds, open their page scans, and confirm the transcription, date and place match the claim.

builds_on: jesse waites' antiquity toolkit (license to check); globalise's transcriptions of the voc archives; delpher's dutch newspapers
why_now: big archives were only machine-transcribed in the last few years, and cheap models can now screen millions of passages for a few dollars. one person proved the method in weeks; the leads still need people who read old dutch, portuguese or spanish, and specialists to judge them.
needs_humans: readers of old dutch, portuguese, spanish and other archive languages to check transcriptions; volcano, meteorite and natural-history specialists to judge leads; people to point the pipeline at new archives.
